intro: Naples has more catalogued monumental trees than any other Italian city, and it keeps them in two places worth a morning each. The Real Bosco di Capodimonte is a former Bourbon hunting estate the royal court spent two centuries filling with specimens from China, Mexico and Australia, and eight of the trees here grow inside it. The second walk is the Real Orto Botanico on Via Foria, founded by decree of Joseph Bonaparte in 1807, where five more stand within 150 metres of each other, including the widest trunk on the city's register. The rest are scattered: a cloister platano regrown from its felled root, a plane on the seafront, and a pine Italy loved so much it replanted after losing the original.
meta_description: Naples's most remarkable trees, in two walks: the Bourbon estate at Capodimonte with its 220-year-old camphor, and the 1807 botanical garden on Via Foria.
question_meta: Naples's oldest tree is a 220-year-old camphor at Capodimonte's Garden of the Princes, brought from China by the Bourbons. Its story and sixteen more trees.

faq_index_1.q: Why does Capodimonte have so many of Naples's oldest trees?
faq_index_1.a: Because the Bourbon kings spent roughly two centuries turning a royal hunting estate into a working botanical showcase, importing camphor from China, cypress from Mexico and eucalyptus from Australia. Eight of the seventeen trees on this list, and more than half of Naples's officially catalogued monumental trees citywide, grow within its 134 hectares.

faq_index_3.q: Are Naples's remarkable trees free to see?
faq_index_3.a: Most are, standing in free public parks, squares and a state archive courtyard. The Real Bosco di Capodimonte's outdoor gardens are free, though its museum and some restored sections keep separate hours. The Real Orto Botanico is also free and needs no booking, but it opens on weekdays only, until 14:00 on Monday, Wednesday and Friday and 16:00 on Tuesday and Thursday, so the five trees there cannot be seen at a weekend.
